newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM tries to draw old allies into coalition.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM tries to draw old allies into coalition.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto met his old allies on Monday to try to convince them to join a new governing coalition after voters denied his Liberal Democratic Party a clear mandate in general elections.
Behind the scenes, Hashimoto aides negotiated with up to 10 possible defectors from the main opposition party Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) to try to persuade them to switch allegiance to the LDP.
"I believe the number of Shinshinto members that will cross over is in the double digits," senior LDP official Shizuka Kamei said in a televised interview.
Hashimoto also held a hand out to the second largest opposition group, the Democratic Party, for them to join a possible four-party coalition he is trying to stitch together.
"The important thing is to stress what is common between us and other politicians, either as individuals or a group, to work together," Hashimoto told a news conference.
The LDP secured 239 seats in Sunday's voting, 12 short of the 251 it needed to govern alone in the 500-seat Lower House.

After a series of funding scandals, the LDP was toppled from power in 1993 after almost 38 years of single-party government. It came back to government in a coalition one year later and Hashimoto took over as prime minister in January.

Commenting on Sunday's results, Hashimoto said: "The result means we have not regained the full confidence of the people. It means we have not been given a full score in our three-year effort to reform ourselves and that we must try even harder."

Parliamentary sources expect coalition negotiations to be protracted as potential partners would make policy demands as conditions for joining an LDP alliance, and the process would have to be drawn out to win over defectors from Shinshinto.
Parliament is likely to convene in early November to formally re-appoint Hashimoto as prime minister, by which time the new government lineup is expected to be finalised.
But some analysts warn the number of interests involved in a new coalition guarantees long-term political uncertainty.

"The political situation will remain unstable and weak government will continue," said political commentator Minoru Morita. "The main point in Japanese politics now is how soon or how late the next elections will be held."
Hashimoto's first priority was to bring on board the leaders of the other parties in the outgoing three-way coalition -- Sakigake's Shoichi Ide and Takako Doi of the Social Democrats.

Sakigake, with just two seats in the lower chamber, has shown it is keen to stay in the ruling camp. But the Social Democrats, with 15 in the Lower House and a critical 32 in the Upper House -- where the LDP is weak, remained noncommittal.
"It is difficult to have cooperative relations with the LDP if things are the same as they used to be," Doi told reporters after meeting Hashimoto.
Hashimoto said he wanted to keep the coalition together, but also hinted that he would like to talk to the newly formed Democratic Party, with its key bloc of 52 seats.
Although the LDP missed a majority, the election left the splintered opposition in disarray. Shinshinto secured 156 seats, four fewer than before.

"If he can pull together independents, Shinshinto rebels, and small groups, none of those would have enough strength to pull down the government," said John Neuffer, a political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute.
Newspapers urged the LDP to accept its limited mandate humbly and blamed all big parties for a record-low turnout of just over 59 percent.

"The LDP should not get too full of itself," the liberal daily Asahi Shimbun said in an editorial. "Not only did it fail to win a majority under an electoral system that favoured the ruling party, it was overall political stability -- rather than specific policies -- that the voters chose."
